I like it, but anybody I pitched it to was like: 'Ewww, TypeScript for Infra.' Pulumi for months used deprecated Azure stuff, and they didn't fix it. So, you are always late to the game, unlike when using plain Terraform.

I used to love Pulumi - the experience of managing infra + k8s resources with Typescript's type system is really nice. However, I've found their support responsiveness via Slack / GH issues to be poor enough to where I'm strongly considering removing it.
We switched to Pulumi from terraform for a new project because we can use it for both cloud infrastructure and for k8s configuration.
Switched from nixops to pulumi, found it much easier to use.
I'm absolutely in love with pulumi. Recommended it to a CTO I was interviewing with literally an hour ago!
I love Pulumi. It's a joy to use a proper programming language to manage infra. I wish more tools would adapt this.

Using Pulumi for about 1 year to manage gcp and AWS environments (5+) - each deployment is around 500 resources. At the begining it was buggy but when they started to add typing i see a lot of improvment.
I'm in love with Pulumi. Simply one of the best tools I have in my stack. After about a year of use, I simply cannot go back to editing YAML files or clicking things in a web UI.
Last time I checked... Pulumi only works by calling in to the mothership: i.e. you cannot build an airgapped infrastructure with it. This was very off-putting for me.

I'm sorry, I really liked Pulumi, but it became too complex after a short while. Since all infra resources are defined as code you end up defining them in a procedural manner (Python), and struggle to arrange/resolve dependencies.
Twice I've tried to love Pulumi but wind up going back to Terraform because the Terraform provider docs put clear usage examples front and center.

A couple of years ago I started down the Pulumi path... values that are only available in the second phase (eg a subnet ID) can't be accessed in the first phase directly... you essentially need to push through source code to be 'eval'ed on the other side.

We've had a chance to try out Pulumi when it was in private beta. We are very happy with it so far. This is the first time I ever had an engineer say to me: 'I really like it, I hope we can keep using it.'
I wish this worked on bare metal. The options for running on premise cloud are slim to none... I don't want to just be another customer for DO, AWS, Azure, etc.
We've now got the same stack structure going with Pulumi and Digital Ocean, having the same ease of development with at least 60% cost reduction versus AWS/CDK.
Pulumi genAI-based documentation is trashed. I've moved to terraform and i was able to achieve much better results in shorter time thanks to higher documentation level for terraform.
Pulumi is really a royal piece of shit. Why the f*ck am I writing code to do 'deployment'... The whole need to figure out when and when not to use Apply. Give me Terraform any day.

I ended up switching to Terraform because the quality of documentation was far superior... I appreciated that their documentation is based a lot on their LLM, however I started to figure out soon that it was plagued with the same issues with other LLMs.
Pulumi maintains its own state service (with option of self management)... As a developer, I quite liked Pulumi resource model, documentation and team responsiveness on Github and slack channel.
Pulumi also has a killer Automation feature, where you can code infrastructure migrations, not unlike you'd do for SQL. Neither TF nor CDK allows you to do that.
